body.heading: A surprisingly gentle force
paragraphs: Here is a humbling thought: a small fridge magnet can lift a paperclip against the gravitational pull of the entire planet Earth. By the standards of physics, gravity is astonishingly weak.

But gravity has two superpowers. It always attracts, never cancels out, and it works over unlimited distances. Every speck of mass adds its pull to every other speck, and given enough mass, the feeble force becomes irresistible.

body.heading: From apples to orbits
paragraphs: Newton realised that the force pulling an apple to the ground is the same force holding the Moon in orbit around Earth. One law, working in the orchard and in the heavens alike.

Einstein later gave us a deeper picture: mass bends the space around it, and objects follow those bends. On that view, Earth does not so much pull the Moon as guide it along a curved path — a description that predicts things Newton’s version cannot, and that your phone’s GPS quietly relies on.

body.heading: Gravity the builder
paragraphs: Left to itself, gravity gathers. It pulls thin gas into clouds, clouds into stars, stars into galaxies, and it is still sculpting the universe’s largest structures today.
The weakest force turns out to be the great architect — not because it is strong, but because it is patient, universal, and never switches off.

takeaway: Gravity is feeble between small things but unstoppable at cosmic scale — the universe’s patient builder.
